Pk and WindowDiff: how far a segmentation's boundaries are from a reference

Source: R/doc-segment-quality.R
gr_seg_pk.Rd

Both slide a window of k positions along two boundary sequences of the same length and count the windows where they disagree, as a share of the L - k + 1 windows of a sequence of length L. gr_seg_pk() (Beeferman, Berger and Lafferty 1999) counts a window as an error when one sequence has a boundary in it and the other has none. gr_seg_windowdiff() (Pevzner and Hearst 2002) counts it when the two have a different number of boundaries in it, so it also sees a window where the hypothesis puts two boundaries and the reference one. Both are 0 for identical sequences and rise towards 1; lower is better.

Usage

gr_seg_pk(reference, hypothesis, k = NULL)

gr_seg_windowdiff(reference, hypothesis, k = NULL)

Arguments

reference, hypothesis

Boundary sequences of the same length: strings of "0" and "1", or vectors of 0 and 1 (or TRUE and FALSE), as gr_seg_boundaries() returns.

k

The window, a whole number from 1 to the sequence length. NULL takes the default above, which needs at least one reference boundary.

Value

One number from 0 to 1, with the window used as attribute k.

Details

These are the definitions of NLTK's pk() and windowdiff(), with the same windows and the same default k, round(L / (2 * boundaries)), rounded half to even as Python rounds. That is NLTK's approximation of half the mean reference segment length. Half the mean length itself, as Beeferman et al. define k, is (L + 1) / (2 * (boundaries + 1)), since L positions describe L + 1 units in boundaries + 1 segments. For "0100" the default is 2: the reference has 5 units in 2 segments, a mean length of 2.5, and half of that, 1.25, would round to 1. Give k to use that figure.

The default k matches NLTK's except in one case: when every position of the reference is a boundary, round(L / (2 * L)) is round(0.5), which is 0. NLTK then uses a window of 0 positions and returns 0 for any hypothesis; this function raises k to 1. With that exception, and whenever k is given, values agree with NLTK's on the same strings.

They measure whether chunk edges fall where topics change. A chunker held to a token cap much smaller than the topics has to cut inside them, and both measures count those cuts as errors; that is a cost of the size as much as of the segmenter, so compare segmenters at one size.

References

Beeferman, D., Berger, A. and Lafferty, J. (1999). Statistical models for text segmentation. Machine Learning 34, 177-210.

Pevzner, L. and Hearst, M. A. (2002). A critique and improvement of an evaluation metric for text segmentation. Computational Linguistics 28(1), 19-36.

See also

gr_seg_boundaries(), gr_seg_recall()

Other segmentation functions: gr_check_segmenter(), gr_chunk_stats(), gr_chunks, gr_register_segmenter(), gr_seg_boundaries(), gr_seg_recall(), gr_segment(), gr_segment_spec(), gr_segmenters(), new_chunks()

Examples

gr_seg_pk("000100000010", "000010000100", k = 3)
#> [1] 0.3
#> attr(,"k")
#> [1] 3
gr_seg_windowdiff("000100000010", "000010000100", k = 3)
#> [1] 0.3
#> attr(,"k")
#> [1] 3
# A window where the hypothesis has one boundary and the reference two is
# an error for WindowDiff only.
gr_seg_pk("0110", "0100", k = 2)
#> [1] 0.3333333
#> attr(,"k")
#> [1] 2
gr_seg_windowdiff("0110", "0100", k = 2)
#> [1] 0.6666667
#> attr(,"k")
#> [1] 2
